video_title: Race to Save Humanity: Inside $12B Colossal Biosciences & $3.8B Astromech
gist: Colossal Biosciences founder Ben Lamm walks through the company's $635M funding history (each round 2x+ oversubscribed) and reframes its business model away from de-extinction novelty toward a broader 'civilization tech' platform monetizing invasive-species eradication (screwworm, gene drives), bio-banking/cloning (the ViaGen acquisition), lab-grown animal materials, and an AI-native drug-discovery spinout, Astromec, built on evolutionary genomics (e.g., elephant p53 cancer resistance) rather than frontier-scale compute.

insights.claim: Colossal Biosciences has raised $635M in total funding; its most recent round was originally targeted at $200M but was oversubscribed to $400M, evidence of strong demand for the platform beyond its headline-grabbing de-extinction PR.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A biotech platform company with no near-term product-sale revenue model is commanding repeat 2x-oversubscribed mega-rounds, signaling investors are pricing in optionality across multiple downstream business lines, not just the mammoth narrative.
insights.quote: 635 total. The last round was supposed to be 200 and it got over subscribed to 400.

insights.claim: Every one of Colossal's funding rounds has been more than 2x oversubscribed, which Lamm interprets as evidence the company has systematically underpriced its equity and may raise its valuation/terms on future rounds.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Signals founder-perceived room to raise future rounds at meaingfully higher prices; existing investors in prior rounds may be sitting on notable unrealized markups by the next raise.
insights.quote: every single round of capital has been more than 2x overs subscribed so what I hear from that is we're cheap.

insights.claim: Colossal deliberately avoided sovereign-scale strategic capital (e.g., SoftBank/Masayoshi Son) early on, instead recruiting long-duration, impact-oriented backers such as Jim Breyer, Thomas Tull, and Mark Walter who could underwrite a 10-50 year technology horizon rather than a typical 4-5 year fund-return timeline.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A cap table selected for patience over speed reduces pressure for premature monetization or a rushed exit, which matters for evaluating governance risk in long-gestation biotech platforms.

insights.claim: Lamm attributes Colossal's fundraising success partly to a prior track record of building and profitably exiting other companies, which gave early investors confidence despite the company initially having no in-house scientists, no university partnerships, and no proven technology.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Founder pedigree from unrelated prior exits was a stronger initial signal to capital than the underlying science itself in a pre-product, pre-team deep-tech raise.
insights.quote: we have no scientist we have no partnership with Harvard um we have no technologies um and and we're a handful of software and hardware people that are pretty they have no background in biology

insights.claim: Colossal explicitly states it is not in the business of selling de-extinct or engineered animals to the public; despite heavy consumer demand (including requests to buy woolly mice), commercial revenue is being built around government/institutional use cases instead.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Investors should not model Colossal as a pet/novelty-animal seller; the addressable market is B2G/B2B licensing and services, which changes the revenue timeline and margin profile versus a consumer product story.
insights.quote: we're not in the selling animal business

insights.claim: Lamm frames Colossal's underlying genome-engineering, DNA-synthesis, and artificial-womb technologies as belonging to a new 'civilization tech' category — infrastructure-level technologies with societal ripple effects beyond a normal product/market, the same category he places companies like Anthropic in.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: This is the framing investors are being sold to justify Colossal's early-stage valuation multiples — comparable to how AI infrastructure players are valued on societal/platform potential rather than near-term unit economics.
insights.quote: there's a new term called civilization tech.

insights.claim: Invasive-species control (rats on islands, screwworm in US cattle, ticks spreading Lyme disease) is characterized as a roughly half-a-trillion-dollar global problem that Colossal's gene-drive and biocontainment technology is positioned to address as a safer alternative to chemical pesticides.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Sizes a large, government-fundable near-term commercial vertical for Colossal that is independent of and less speculative than full species de-extinction.
insights.quote: invasive species is like half a trillion dollar problem globally.

insights.claim: In the New World screwworm outbreak affecting Texas cattle, the US government is reportedly spending about $1.5B over an expected 8-year timeline using conventional methods, while Colossal claims its already-built gene-drive solution could eradicate the problem in 6-7 months in every model it has run, pending government permitting.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: If permitted, this is a concrete near-term (sub-1-year) government-procurement opportunity with an explicit taxpayer cost-savings pitch (potentially a decade and billions of dollars) — worth tracking USDA/permitting news as a catalyst.
insights.quote: they're spending a billion five in taxes and in 8 years they're going to like slow or stop the problem.

insights.claim: A company that buys billions of dollars annually of a specific ethically-harvested animal fiber approached Colossal to help scale supply 5-6x; rather than expanding animal harvesting, Colossal is pursuing lab-grown hair/fiber production, already demonstrated by growing mammoth hair from elephant stem-cell-derived follicles.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A previously unmodeled, inbound-demand-driven materials/biomanufacturing revenue line (lab-grown animal fiber at industrial scale) that emerged organically from Colossal's stem-cell tooling, not from its original roadmap.
insights.quote: we actually have uh hair follicles uh growing in and where we've taken elephant stem cells and created follicles so that we can grow mammoth hair.

insights.claim: A Middle East partner with cultural/falconry ties approached Colossal to help revive a critically endangered or semi-extinct bird species after spending billions on their own failed artificial-egg and conservation efforts, illustrating inbound institutional demand for Colossal's avian reproductive technology.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Points to a sovereign-wealth-adjacent, culturally-motivated buyer segment for Colossal's reproductive-biotech services outside the US/Western conservation market.

insights.claim: Components of Colossal's artificial-womb research have direct applications to human IVF and embryo health, and its germline-editing capability could in principle target human genetic disease, but the company has chosen to license or spin out any human-facing application rather than pursue human work in-house.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A large adjacent human-health TAM exists but Colossal is capital-light on it by design (license/spin-out), reducing regulatory/reputational exposure while retaining upside via licensing economics.
insights.quote: our technologies can be applied to human and we can spin them out and license them but we won't do the human work here right

insights.claim: Colossal spun out an AI drug-discovery company, Astromec, which has raised capital recently and may raise again soon, built on evolutionary and comparative genomics rather than broad frontier-model scale.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A capital-raise event to watch in AI-for-biotech; positions Astromec as a distinct investable entity separate from Colossal's core de-extinction business.
insights.quote: raised money recently and may or may not be raising money now soonish

insights.claim: Astromec's model is deliberately narrow rather than broad, so it does not require the massive compute buildouts (Lamm cites roughly $500B-scale data centers) that generalist frontier AI labs need, avoiding competition for power and water resources.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A capital-efficiency thesis against the mega-compute AI infrastructure race — an applied, narrow-domain model can be commercially viable without hyperscaler-level infrastructure spend, relevant to how investors should underwrite AI-biotech capex.
insights.quote: we don't have to go build a $500 billion data center in computing power.

insights.claim: Astromec's core method looks at evolutionary conservation across species to explain disease resistance — e.g., elephants get cancer at roughly 2-3% versus about 24-25% in humans, a difference Lamm attributes to overexpression of the p53 tumor-suppressor protein — and aims to build prediction models applicable to cancer and potentially bird flu.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable scientific thesis underlying an AI-biotech spinout: cross-species comparative genomics as a drug-target discovery engine, differentiated from generic LLM-based drug discovery approaches.
insights.quote: if you look at a protein like p-53 in elephants, elephants get cancer at about a rate of 2 to 3%, humans are about 24 to 25%.

insights.claim: Colossal holds what Lamm describes as the world's largest elephant genomic dataset and the largest multi-species dataset on EHV (elephant herpesvirus, which kills roughly 20% of baby elephants), a proprietary data asset feeding both its conservation work and Astromec's drug-discovery models.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A defensible proprietary-data moat (rather than algorithms alone) underpins Astromec's approach, a durable advantage that is harder for AI-only entrants to replicate quickly.
insights.quote: Like most people don't know that 20% of baby elephants die because of EEHV.

insights.claim: Colossal's 'woolly mice' project produced 100% healthy live births with exactly the predicted phenotypes using the most simultaneous (multiplex) gene edits ever delivered in one procedure, completed in just 30 days from edit design to birth, validating the end-to-end pipeline Colossal intends to use for mammoth de-extinction.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: The 30-day, 100%-success multiplex-edit result is the technical proof point that de-risks Colossal's core platform claim; it's a validation milestone investors can point to independent of PR virality.
insights.quote: we had 100% healthy mice born with exactly the predicted phenotypes

insights.claim: Colossal's edit-complexity has scaled rapidly: investors were told five years ago that doing five-to-seven simultaneous gene edits would be a strong result, but the company is now routinely doing hundreds of edits and is developing a new construct/delivery mechanism targeting thousands of simultaneous edits.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A roughly two-order-of-magnitude jump in editing throughput in under five years is the underlying technical curve that determines feasibility/timeline for full species-level de-extinction — a key metric to track over future funding rounds.
insights.quote: we were told if in five years we were doing five to seven edits we'd be great. We're now doing hundred.

insights.claim: Colossal acquired ViaGen, the leading US animal cloning company, specifically because ViaGen's cloning efficiency (about 80%) vastly outperformed the roughly 2% success rate typical elsewhere in the industry, folding it in as a vertical-integration bolt-on to control the full bio-banking-to-cloning production stack.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: An explicit M&A rationale (buy the best-in-class efficiency asset rather than build from a 2% base rate) that illustrates Colossal's build-vs-buy-vs-license capital allocation logic across its supply chain.
insights.quote: Vioagen had like cloning efficiencies at 80% where most people are at 2% right

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf frontier AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic's Claude were not useful for Colossal's core science (e.g., ancestral genome reconstruction, comparative genomics), forcing the company to build a proprietary in-house AI team and bespoke tooling rather than relying on general-purpose LLMs.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A concrete data point against the 'general LLMs solve every vertical' narrative — specialized scientific domains like comparative genomics still require bespoke model-building, which is relevant to how investors size the AI-services TAM available to generalist model providers versus vertical specialists.
insights.quote: Opus doesn't do like an ancestral state reconstruction of like a genome and like it doesn't like build comparative genomics models.

insights.claim: Colossal's embryology and somatic-cell-nuclear-transfer (cloning) lab work is currently manual but fully screen-recorded and instrumented (tracking laser position, oocyte position, DNA extraction), with the explicit plan to automate the entire workflow with robotics in the future.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A visible roadmap toward robotics-driven throughput scaling in cloning/embryology, which would be a future margin and capacity catalyst worth watching for in company updates.

insights.claim: Original frozen/ancient tissue samples used for de-extinction research are dead cells and cannot be directly cloned; Colossal instead engineers the target genome from scratch using extracted ancient DNA sequence data rather than attempting to clone preserved specimens.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Corrects a common misconception (Jurassic-Park-style cloning from frozen tissue) that could otherwise mislead an investor's mental model of the actual technical process and IP being built.
insights.quote: those tissues are dead. You cannot clone from dead cells.

insights.claim: Lamm's stated 'hottest take' is that AI convergence will enable a real-time 'digital twin of nature' — analogous to missile-defense or tsunami/earthquake prediction models — letting society model the ecological consequences of decisions (e.g., building a data center, diverting a river) before acting.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Signals a future product/data-platform direction for Colossal beyond genome engineering — ecological simulation/prediction infrastructure — that could open a distinct government or enterprise-risk-modeling market.
insights.quote: I think AI is going to converge and uh we are going to build a digital twin of nature

insights.claim: Colossal frames the urgency of its mission around a forecast that up to 50% of all biodiversity could be lost in the next 25 years, positioning de-extinction and gene-banking tools as insurance built ahead of a mass-extinction event rather than as a replacement for conventional conservation.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: This is the core risk narrative underpinning Colossal's entire fundraising and mission pitch to both government and impact-oriented investors.
insights.quote: It's currently forecasted that we're going to lose up to 50% of all biodiversity in the next 25 years.

insights.claim: Colossal argues its work is additive to, not a replacement for, conventional conservation, citing as evidence that funding for its elephant-conservation partners has increased since Colossal's founding, alongside greater public awareness of threats such as EEHV.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable claim (rising conservation-partner funding) that investors or diligence teams could verify directly with named conservation partners to validate the company's net-positive-impact narrative.
insights.quote: if you go talk to any of our elephant conservation partners, they'll tell you that their funding has gone up since Colossal was invented.

insights.claim: Any reintroduction of de-extinct species into the wild, or field deployment of gene-drive/invasive-species technology, is entirely gated by government and indigenous-community approval; Colossal describes actively briefing the USDA, the intelligence community, and the Department of War on these technologies but says deployment decisions rest with those bodies, not the company.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Frames regulatory/permitting timelines (not technical readiness) as the binding constraint on commercialization of Colossal's gene-drive and rewilding technologies — the key catalyst to track is government permitting news, not lab milestones.

insights.claim: Colossal open-sources its technologies specifically for conservation use so that any organization can use them for free for conservation purposes, while reserving the right to pursue legal action against use of its technology for non-conservation ('nefarious') purposes.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: An open-source-for-conservation strategy broadens ecosystem goodwill and adoption while Colossal's core commercial IP (government/enterprise use cases) remains monetized separately — a dual-track IP strategy worth noting for anyone evaluating the company's moat.

themes.theme: Talent, Culture & Brand as Recruiting Moat

insights.claim: Colossal's team comprises roughly 260+ employees, 17 academic institutional partners, about 80 people in academic labs it funds, and roughly 95 advisors split across scientific, indigenous, executive/business, and youth advisory boards, with the youth board treated as institutionally as important as the scientific board.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: The scale and structure of the extended advisor/partner network (beyond headcount) is a meaningful part of Colossal's scientific and stakeholder-management capacity, relevant to assessing organizational execution risk at this stage of growth.
insights.quote: we have 260 plus people plus 17 academic partners plus 80 folks in academic uh labs that we also fund uh and about 95 adviserss.

insights.claim: Colossal deliberately built a distinctive 'Harvard meets MTV' brand aesthetic and non-commercial internal-only branded merchandise specifically as a scientific-talent recruiting tool, arguing it gives an 'unfair advantage' over underfunded, politicized academic labs competing for the same researchers.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Brand/culture investment is being treated as a direct talent-acquisition lever in a market where scientific talent is the binding constraint, not a marketing afterthought — relevant to how investors should read Colossal's spend on facilities/branding.
insights.quote: So how do you take like Harvard meets MTV? That was like our thesis from like day one.

insights.claim: Lamm attributes investor trust in Colossal to a consistent pattern of exceeding its own previously communicated technical roadmap targets (such as edit-count milestones), combined with a decision framework of 'value creation, impact, and inspiration' communicated to investors from the company's first pitch.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A track record of beating self-set milestones is the credibility mechanism enabling Colossal's oversubscribed rounds — a pattern investors can look for continuing (or breaking) in future updates as a signal on execution risk.

insights.claim: Colossal maintains an explicit internal 'no-go' boundary against performing human-focused genetic engineering or non-human-primate research in-house (it will only license or spin out such work), a line drawn in part to avoid fueling existing conspiracy narratives about the company.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: A self-imposed regulatory/reputational firewall that reduces bioethics and PR tail-risk exposure as the company's genome-engineering capability set continues to expand into adjacent, higher-stakes application areas.
insights.quote: our technologies can be applied to human and we can spin them out and license them but we won't do the human work here right

insights.claim: Despite public conspiracy claims linking Colossal to secret government or UAP ('alien') research, Lamm directly denies that any of the company's genome-engineering advances derive from studying non-human or extraterrestrial material.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Notable given Lamm discloses he sits on a UAP-related scientific advisory board and has past imaging work tied to Army Space, which is likely the actual source of the (unfounded) rumor connecting Colossal to UAP research.
insights.quote: the advancements in genome engineering has come from us studying like which is just not the case which is just crazy talk.

insights.claim: Public engagement moments like the animatronic direwolf lobby display and the woolly-mice reveal are deliberate brand/inspiration tools rather than genuine access to live specimens; Colossal keeps its actual de-extinct and endangered-species animals off public display for security reasons after unauthorized visitors showed up seeking to see them in person.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm, Colossal Biosciences CEO
insights.so_what: Physical biosecurity and access control around Colossal's live genetic assets is an operational risk factor investors should note as the company's public profile and specimen inventory both grow.
